title: Remove, disassemble and install engine system components of agricultural equipment

lessons.title: Engine systems and safe preparation
lessons.html:
The engine systems

Most farm tractors, bakkies and pumps have diesel engines. An engine has several systems. Each system has parts you may need to remove and fit:

  • Fuel system – tank, lift pump, fuel filters, injector pump, injectors, pipes.
  • Cooling system – radiator, water pump, thermostat, fan, hoses.
  • Lubrication system – oil pump, oil filter, oil cooler, sump.
  • Air intake and exhaust – air filter, turbocharger, manifolds, silencer.
  • Starting and charging – starter motor, alternator, belts.

Getting ready

  1. Read the workshop manual for the engine model. Note torque values and special tools.
  2. Park on level ground, switch off, take the key out and disconnect the battery negative cable.
  3. Let the engine cool down completely.
  4. Get drip trays, clean containers, caps and plugs to close open pipes.
  5. Wear gloves, safety glasses and safety boots.

Dangers to watch

  • Hot parts – manifolds, turbo and coolant can burn.
  • High-pressure fuel – fuel from an injector pipe can go through your skin. Never feel for a leak with your hand. Get medical help at once if fuel gets into the skin.
  • Fire – diesel on a hot engine can catch fire. Keep a fire extinguisher near and no smoking.
  • Fans and belts – never put your hand near them with the engine running.

lessons.title: Removing and taking apart engine parts
lessons.html:
Keep dirt out

Dirt is the enemy of an engine. One grain of sand in a fuel injector can stop it working. Before you open anything, clean the area around it with a brush and degreaser. As soon as you take a pipe off, close it with a clean cap or plug. Never use a rag to plug a fuel pipe – fibres get inside.

Removing a part

  1. Drain the fluid first, for example coolant before you take off the water pump. Catch it in a tray.
  2. Take photos and put tags on hoses, pipes and wires.
  3. Loosen belt tension before you remove an alternator or water pump.
  4. Undo the bolts evenly. Keep bolts with the part, because some are different lengths.
  5. Lift the part off. Get help or a hoist for heavy parts like a starter or a turbo.

Disassembling on the bench

Only take apart what the manual says you may. Some parts, like an injector pump, must go to a specialist diesel workshop.

Lay parts out in order on a clean bench. Look for:

  • cracked or warped housings;
  • worn bearings or bushes;
  • leaking seals and hard gaskets;
  • blocked radiator fins or corroded water pump vanes;
  • a thermostat that does not open in hot water when you test it as the manual shows.

Write all faults on the job card and give it to your supervisor.

lessons.title: Installing engine parts and checking
lessons.html:
Installing

  1. Clean the mating faces. Scrape off old gasket without scratching the metal.
  2. Use new gaskets, seals and O-rings from the parts list.
  3. Fit the part and start all bolts by hand so threads do not cross.
  4. Tighten in the order shown in the manual, with a torque wrench, to the right torque.
  5. Connect hoses, pipes and wires using your tags and photos.
  6. Set the belt tension as the manual shows. A loose belt slips; a too-tight belt damages bearings.
  7. Refill coolant or oil with the type in the manual.

Bleeding the fuel system

If you opened the fuel system, air gets in and the engine will not run. Bleed it as the manual says, usually with the hand primer on the lift pump, opening the bleed screws in order. Catch spilled diesel with a rag and clean it up.

Checking the job

  • Reconnect the battery and start the engine.
  • Check the oil pressure light goes out.
  • Look for leaks of fuel, oil and coolant.
  • Let it reach working temperature and watch the temperature gauge.
  • Switch off, let it cool, and check the coolant and oil levels again.

Clean up, store used fluids for recycling and fill in the job card.

Key points

  • Let the engine cool and disconnect the battery before you start.
  • Keep dirt out: clean first and cap every open pipe.
  • Never feel for a high-pressure fuel leak with your hand.
  • Use new gaskets and seals and tighten to the manual torque.
  • Bleed the fuel system and check for leaks after the job.
